summary: This note lists ten bizarre folk customs and festivals from around the world, from goat tossing in Alcántara to the Monkey Buffet Festival in Lopburi. Each entry gives the place, date, and a short description of the ritual and its supposed origin or meaning. The note frames these customs as expressions of cultural identity, continuity, and the human desire to celebrate and honor history.
one_line: A roundup of ten quirky folk festivals worldwide, including radish carving, baby jumping, orange battles, and cheese rolling, and what they say about tradition.
key_facts: The Goat Tossing Festival in Alcántara, Spain, takes place every 12th of September during the Festival of San Vincente de Martir; a young goat is tossed from the church belfry, and many advocate that it is now thrown onto a protective tarp.

La Noche de los Rábanos (Night of the Radishes) is held on December 23rd in Oaxaca, Mexico, where artisans carve intricate sculptures entirely from radishes, with a competition for the best creations.
The Boryeong Mud Festival runs July 17th to July 27th at Daecheon Beach in South Korea; it began as a marketing event for Boryeong mud cosmetics and now attracts millions.

El Colacho in Castrillo de Murcia, Spain, has men dressed as devils leap over rows of newborn babies to cleanse them of original sin; it occurs on the first Sunday after Corpus Christi and has been practiced since the 1620s.

The Battle of the Oranges in Ivrea, Italy, runs February 14th through February 16th, with thousands of participants in nine combat teams throwing oranges to commemorate defiance against an evil marquis.

The Festival of Exploding Hammers in San Juan de la Vega, Mexico, is held February 28th; men attach sulfa and chlorate to sledgehammers and slam them against rail beams to cause explosions, supposedly honoring Saint John the Baptist for aiding miners against an oppressive baron.
The Cooper's Hill Cheese-Rolling and Wake in Gloucestershire, England, is held on the last Monday of May, when contestants chase an 8-pound wheel of Double Gloucester cheese down a steep hill.

El Salto del Colacho in Vilariño de Conso, Spain, is held on January 23rd, with men dressed as devils jumping over babies born during the previous year to bring them good luck and protect them from illness.

The Testicle Festival ('Testy Festy') in Clinton, Montana, is held the first weekend of August and serves bull testicles, or 'Rocky Mountain Oysters', paying homage to livestock castration in the local ranching community.

The Monkey Buffet Festival in Lopburi, Thailand, is held on the last Sunday of November, with over 2,000 kilograms of fruits, vegetables, cakes, and candies laid out for the local macaques living in the ancient city's ruins.
Animal rights groups have called for the discontinuation of the Alcántara goat tossing, which has come under scrutiny.
The note argues these customs, though odd, reflect the human desire to celebrate, honor history, and continue age-old practices.
